text: Every time Northbridge hires an engineer or spins up a server, someone runs through the same setup steps by hand: create the account, drop in an SSH key, fix the permissions. This lesson scripts that, with one hard requirement -- it has to be safe to run twice, because someone will run it twice.

A script that blindly runs useradd works the first time and fails the second, because the user already exists. An idempotent script checks the current state first and only changes what needs changing. id -u exits non-zero if the user doesn't exist, so that check decides whether to create the account at all.

The same idea applies to the SSH key: grep checks whether it's already in authorized_keys before appending, so rerunning the script doesn't paste the same key in twice. Permissions get fixed unconditionally on every run, because sshd silently refuses a key if the directory isn't 700 or the file isn't 600.

Three checks do the real work: id -u before creating the user, grep -qF before appending the key, and unconditional chmod and chown to self-heal permissions every time, even when they're already correct. usermod -aG is naturally idempotent too -- adding someone to a group they're already in is a no-op.

Northbridge's engineers touch more than one server, so a Python wrapper runs the bash script over SSH on each one and checks subprocess's returncode. A non-zero code gets logged by server name instead of silently skipped, so a failure shows up immediately instead of weeks later when someone can't log in.

Idempotency is the rule that makes a setup script trustworthy enough to hand off: check state, change only what's wrong, and run it as many times as needed. Next, lesson 19 turns that same fleet-wide approach toward parsing logs and building a report.
